b:
With nominal U.S. home prices near record highs and 30-year fixed-rate mortgages exceeding 7%, many prospective homebuyers are debating: should I buy a home or keep renting? I know this because I'm one of them.
Back in 2024, I ran the numbers on buying vs. renting and concluded that I would "remain a renter for the foreseeable future." Well, it's been two years and I'm still renting. Though U.S. home prices are technically 3.9% below their 2022 peak (after inflation), nominal prices remain high and rates have gone up slightly since 2024.
The math says I should keep renting based on my local housing market ($4,650/month to rent vs. ~$10,000/month all-in to buy). But I've started to wonder: can I do this forever?
It's easy to justify renting when the circumstances make sense. Maybe rates are too high or prices have gotten a little ahead of themselves. But what if things never revert? What will I do in that scenario? Though the math suggests that I should be better off financially as a renter, what kind of risks does this entail?
Renting for a few years is one thing, but what are the tradeoffs of renting for the long haul? Let's find out.

Before we look at the downsides of being a forever renter, let's examine some of the primary benefits. Most of these benefits hold in any housing market, but the first one is based on today's higher rates and prices:

More Wealth: All else equal, you would expect to end up with more wealth over the next few decades by being a renter (and investing the excess cash you save) versus borrowing and buying at today's rates and prices. This is because the money you save on your mortgage, taxes, insurance, and maintenance (relative to your rent) can compound over time and build more overall wealth. The best way to check, though, is to run the numbers.

More Predictability: Even without running the numbers, renting has another clear advantage over buying—predictability. As the saying goes, "Rent is the most you’ll pay for housing. A mortgage is the least you’ll pay." Renters know how much they will pay for housing through the end of their lease term. Homeowners have no such assurances.

While a mortgage is a predictable expense, property taxes, insurance, and maintenance are anything but. Property taxes and insurance tend to rise over time, sometimes sharply. And while many experts recommend budgeting 1% of your home's value annually for maintenance, such costs are rarely linear. For example, one year you may spend almost nothing on home maintenance while in another you spend a few percent of your home's value on a new roof or A/C unit. So while the average cost is around 1% (of home value) per year, you can't predict how much you might spend in any given year.

Less Hassle: When you're a renter, you don't have to worry about fixing anything on the property. That's your landlord's responsibility. They have to spend their time and money to repair the property while you live your life. This is why many homeowners jokingly call homeownership a part-time job. Less hassle becomes even more valuable as you age. After all, do you want to deal with replacing your water heater when you're 80?

Increased Optionality: Given the transaction costs associated with buying a home, it only makes financial sense if you plan on living there for many years. As a renter, you have no such long-term lock-in. If you lose your job or need to move away due to an unforeseen circumstance, you can. Yes, a homeowner could do the same thing by selling their home, but renters are far more mobile in this regard. That optionality is worth something, especially if you don't have your life figured out yet.

More Diversification and Liquidity: When you buy a home, you are essentially placing a leveraged bet on an illiquid real estate position. And since most homeowners have a large portion of their wealth tied up in their home, this ends up being a concentrated position as well. However, when you rent, you have no such concentrated bet and can keep your wealth both diversified and liquid for future opportunities.
Taken together, all of these benefits make a compelling case for long-term renting. But they don't come without serious costs.
Despite the pros of long-term renting, it has some lesser-known issues that become more apparent with time:

Less Housing Selection: When we compare renting and buying, we implicitly assume that the housing quality is the same in both cases. Unfortunately, that isn’t always the case. While 13.7% of single-family homes nationally are renter-occupied, they aren't evenly spread out across the country. According to Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies, more than a third of America's neighborhoods are "rental deserts" where less than 20% of housing is available for rent. And these rental deserts have a median household income of $99,670 compared to only $53,170 for areas with robust rental options.

In other words, the nicest neighborhoods generally have the lowest rental supply. This is particularly pronounced where I live in the New York metro area, where only 4.3% of rentals are single-family homes, the lowest among the top 50 metros. So, if you want to be a forever renter, don't expect to be able to get into every neighborhood.

Less Stability/Control: What the renter gains in optionality, they give up in stability and control. I've moved over 10 times in the last decade as a renter and will have to move again in the future. A homeowner has control and stability over their housing in a way that a renter never will.

Requires More Discipline: If you want to come out ahead as a long-term renter (vs. a homeowner), you need to be able to save any excess money (from your cheaper rent) and invest it every month for decades without selling. Without such discipline, you could end up worse off than a homeowner who just paid their mortgage each month. This is a huge behavioral benefit of owning your own home—forced savings via your mortgage that you can't easily sell during an economic downturn. Sometimes, illiquidity is a feature, not a bug.
You Always Need Housing: One thing that makes buying a home different from any other financial transaction is that you always need housing. This tweet from Ben Southwood solidified this idea for me:

I am structurally short housing, because I am always going to want to consume some at any given time in the future. If I own approximately as much housing as I want to consume then I am neutral on housing; if I own more, then I am long; if I own less, then I am short.

Shorting housing seems riskier to me than being neutral on it. In fact, since I probably want to consume more housing in the future when I'm hopefully richer, I should probably even go long. If housing falls in price then what I lose in investment I gain in housing consumption, whereas if housing *rises* in price and I don't own any then I am doubly hit!

This is the primary benefit of being a homeowner—you know with certainty you already have your housing covered in the future. The renter, on the other hand, always has to go into the marketplace and accept the market price for housing. So while your rent may be low now, there's no guarantee it will be low later. And where I live, this risk is already materializing. Since mid-2022, home prices in the New York metro area have increased about 13% after inflation, even as real prices have fallen nationally.

Many benefits of long-term renting have a mirrored cost. Increased optionality comes with less stability and control. More wealth requires more financial discipline. More liquidity means less protection from your own behavior.
For a few years, it's easy to accept these tradeoffs. But to do it for a lifetime is a different thing altogether.

Whether you decide to buy or rent for the long term is a complex decision based on a host of factors. And while I can't speak for anyone else, I know I won't be a renter within a few years.
Even if mortgage rates and housing prices remain elevated, at some point I have to live my life. Of course, money is important, but stability for my family is even more important. So, in the balance between being a renter and a homeowner, homeownership tips the scales.
Why? Because of what Southwood articulated—I will almost certainly need more housing in the future. So if I buy and prices drop, I'll be happy to buy more housing. But if I don't buy and prices keep going up, I'm putting my family in a tough spot.
So, is it better to rent forever? If you value optionality, less hassle, diversification, and (possibly) more wealth, it can be. But if you value stability, neighborhood selection, and knowing your housing is always covered, ownership is hard to beat. For years, I valued renting more. But now that I have a family, I'm ready to own, even if the math suggests otherwise.
Renting was always my plan for the foreseeable future. But that future is coming to an end.
